reason: The sources contain rich, multi-verified historical facts regarding France's deadliest rail disaster, its causes, and the 90-year cover-up.
story: On December 12, 1917, nearly 1,000 French soldiers boarded military train 612, returning home from the Italian front for Christmas leave. At Modane station, the driver objected to taking the massive, 19-coach train down a steep Alpine gradient with only a single locomotive, but a transport officer overruled him. Cruelly, most officers then abandoned the train to ride the Modane-Paris express. With only three coaches equipped with air brakes, the overloaded train accelerated to a terrifying 135 km/h. It derailed on a sharp curve, and the wooden coaches ignited from overheated brakes and candles. Over 600 men perished. The next morning, only 183 soldiers answered roll call. Desperate to protect their officers, the French military classified the disaster for 90 years, heavily censoring the press. While civilian railway workers were court-martialed and acquitted, the deadly military operational failure remained buried in the dark.
angle: To protect military commanders who overloaded a troop train and then abandoned it for an express, the French military kept the deadliest train crash in France's history a classified secret for 90 years.

claims.claim: The Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne derailment took place on December 12, 1917.

evidence.quote: The Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne derailment of December 12, 1917, was a railway accident
The Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne derailment of December 12, 1917, was a railway accident

claims.claim: The train was carrying French soldiers returning home for leave from the Italian front in World War I.

evidence.quote: involving a troop train carrying at least 1,000 French soldiers on their way home for leave from the Italian front in World War I.

Nearly a thousand French soldiers, crammed into 19 Italian-built coaches, had survived a month reinforcing the Italian front after the Battle of Caporetto. Now, on the night of December 12, 1917, military train number 612 was threading its way down the Maurienne valley toward Chambery, where the men would scatter across France for 15 days of holiday leave.

claims.claim: It is the deadliest railway accident in French history.

evidence.quote: It is France's deadliest rail accident to date
The derailment remains the deadliest rail catastrophe in French history

claims.claim: Most of the officers left the train at Modane to take the Modane-Paris express.

evidence.quote: Most of the officers left the train during this stop, to take the Modane-Paris express.
Most of the officers had already left at Modane, transferring to the Paris express.

claims.claim: The train was 350 meters long and weighed over 500 tonnes.

evidence.quote: for a total length of 350 metres and total weight of 526 tonnes.
The train weighed 526 tonnes, stretched 350 metres long

claims.claim: The train had only a single locomotive instead of the normal two because the second was requisitioned.

evidence.quote: Such a train normally would have had two engines. However, the second assigned locomotive had been requisitioned for a munitions train by the officer in charge of dispatching.
Such a train normally would have had two engines. However, the second assigned locomotive had been requisitioned for a munitions train by the officer in charge of dispatching.

claims.claim: The driver objected to taking the heavy load with a single engine but was overruled by the transport officer.

evidence.quote: The driver objected to taking the heavy load with a single engine, but was overruled by the transport officer.
The driver objected to taking the heavy load with a single engine, but was overruled by the transport officer.

claims.claim: Only the first three coaches had air brakes, while the rest had hand brakes or no brakes.

evidence.quote: Of those coaches, only the first three had air brakes, the remaining coaches had only hand brakes or no brakes at all.
Of those coaches, only the first three had air brakes, the remaining coaches had only hand brakes or no brakes at all.

claims.claim: The train accelerated down the steep mountain descent to an uncontrollable speed of 135 km/h.

evidence.quote: accelerating to an eventual uncontrollable speed of 135 km/h (84 mph) as measured by the locomotive's speed indicator.
accelerating to an eventual uncontrollable speed of 135km/h as measured by the locomotive's speed indicator.

claims.claim: The first coach derailed at 102 km/h where the authorized speed limit was 40 km/h.

evidence.quote: The first coach derailed at 102 km/h (63 mph) where the authorized speed was 40 km/h (25 mph)
The first coach derailed at 102km/h where the authorized speed was 40km/h

claims.claim: The wooden coaches caught fire due to overheated brakes and lit candles.

evidence.quote: The wooden coaches smashed into one another and promptly caught fire, caused by the overheated brakes and lit candles which had been brought aboard
The wooden wagons ignited by the overheated brakes and also by the candles used to light the wagons.

claims.claim: Thirty-seven bodies of soldiers who had jumped from the runaway train were found along the tracks.

evidence.quote: 37 more bodies were found strewn along the ballast of the railway or the right-of-way, between La Praz and the metal bridge, belonging to soldiers who had jumped off the out-of-control train
Some soldiers jumped from the careening coaches; 37 of their bodies were later found strewn along the tracks.

claims.claim: Only 183 men reported for roll call the morning after the disaster.

evidence.quote: Only 183 men who had been on the train reported for roll-call on the next morning (December 13).
When roll call was taken on the morning of December 13, only 183 men answered their names.

claims.claim: The disaster was kept as a classified military secret for 90 years.

evidence.quote: The accident remained a classified military secret for 90 years.
The disaster remained effectively classified for 90 years

claims.claim: The French daily Le Figaro devoted only 21 lines to the accident four days after it occurred.

evidence.quote: The daily Le Figaro devoted only 21 lines to the accident on December 17, four days after the accident.
Le Figaro, one of France's leading newspapers, devoted exactly 21 lines to the accident, four days after it happened.

claims.claim: A court-martial tried six employees of the PLM railway company and acquitted them.

evidence.quote: A court-martial was called to try six employees of the PLM (Paris–Lyon–Mediterranée) railway. They were acquitted.
A court-martial was eventually convened, but it tried six employees of the PLM railway company rather than any military officials. All six were acquitted.

claims.claim: The station master at La Praz warned Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, preventing a head-on collision with a British troop train.

evidence.quote: The station master at La Praz, seeing the train passing at an out-of-control speed, had notified the station master at the next larger station, Saint Jean de Maurienne, who held the departure of a train full of British soldiers, thereby preventing a catastrophic head-on collision.

The station master at La Praz, seeing the train passing at an out-of-control speed, had notified the station master at the next larger station, Saint Jean de Maurienne, who held the departure of a train full of British soldiers, thereby preventing a catastrophic head-on collision.

claims.claim: Both a military hospital and a nearby pasta factory were turned into makeshift hospitals and mortuaries.

evidence.quote: Both the military hospital at Saint Jean de Maurienne and the Bozon-Verduraz pasta factory nearby were transformed into makeshift field hospitals and mortuaries
The military hospital at Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne and the Bozon-Verduraz pasta factory nearby were pressed into service as field hospitals and mortuaries.

claims.claim: In June 1923, André Maginot inaugurated a monument to the victims in the cemetery of Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne.

evidence.quote: On June 6, 1923 the Minister of Defense, André Maginot, inaugurated a monument to the victims in the cemetery of Saint Michel de Maurienne.

In 1923, Defense Minister Andre Maginot -- the same man who would later lend his name to France's famous fortification line -- inaugurated a monument to the victims in the cemetery of Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne.

claims.claim: The train derailment occurred as it descended the steep 3.3% grade between Modane and Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne.

evidence.quote: overloaded for operation on the steep 3.3% grade between Modane (elevation 1040 metres) and Saint Michel de Maurienne (elevation 710 metres)

disputed: The exact death toll of the disaster is disputed: the official declassified report states 435 deaths, while other records and historical estimates place the number between 675 and 800. A script should present this range rather than treating a single figure as absolute.

The popular topic description of a commander forcing the driver at gunpoint is not supported by any of the provided sources, which only state that the driver was overruled by the transport officer. The script must omit any mention of a gunpoint threat to remain historically accurate to the sources.
